doc.title: Warren Bernhardt interviewed by Monk Rowe, Bearsville, New York, January 3, 2012

title: Beethoven as the great improviser
summary: Bernhardt argues Beethoven was a superb improviser and finds jazz in Opus 111.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: good improvisation. I mean most of your great composers in the Eurocentric thing, oh we haven’t even gotten to African music yet. That influence, you know, that’s a whole other thing. But the European, Eurocentric composing community, they were all great improvisers. The greatest of them all, Beethoven, was a superb improviser. That’s my opinion. I think he’s the granddaddy. Some people say Bach but I say Beethoven. And I’ve played enough of him that I think I know, and I’ve listened to him enough. At least for me I’m satisfied that when I approach a piece of his that this is going to be really a challenge, even the simplest piece. This is going to be really something. This was written by a guy who was stone deaf. Start right there. I mean I just did Opus 111, the last 30 seconds, the famous part that’s jazz. It’s written in 29/32nds or something [scats]. And if you play it that way it really makes sense. You see what he intended. I mean he was what, two hundred years before Philly Joe Jones and he was doing the same shit. I mean he’s something else. And all these guys. You don’t get famous — there’s no bogus stuff going on there, you know, becoming immortal or being immortal.
